title: Can Composio build a toolkit for these 100 apps? An agent researched them, then had to prove it.
headlines: 88 of 100 apps are buildable today, and none are technically impossible. The 12 "partial" apps are blocked by commercial gates (a sales contract, an admin approval, an enterprise plan), not by missing APIs. So the bottleneck for the long tail is partnerships and outreach, not engineering.

MCP has become standard: 86 of 100 vendors now publish an official MCP server. Coverage is no longer the question; what matters is whether the vendor's MCP covers the same surface as the API. Several (Coda, Otter, Higgsfield) use OAuth only on the MCP while the REST API uses a different credential.

72% are self-serve for a developer (free tier, free trial or open source). Gating clusters by category: Developer/Infra has zero gated apps, while AI-native, Ecommerce and Finance have the most approval, paid or sales-led access.

Auth is a mix, not a standard: 58% support OAuth2, 52% personal/Bearer tokens, 28% plain API keys, 14% HTTP Basic. Many apps offer two methods (OAuth for multi-tenant apps, a token for single-workspace use), so a toolkit usually needs both.

Accuracy rose from 91% (agent alone) to 96% after the verification loop and audit, measured field-by-field on a 20-app stratified sample. Auth method is the hardest field (85%); MCP was the biggest gain (85% → 100%).
patterns_lead: Patterns across all 100 apps. Each bar is counted from the table below, and every cell in that table links to its source.
heat_note: Read across a row: green = a developer can start today, amber/red = someone has to approve or sell you access. Developer and productivity tools are almost all green; finance, AI-native and ecommerce carry most of the gates.
wins_note: Self-serve, broad API, buildable now: the fastest toolkits to ship.
outreach_note: Blocked by access, not technology: these need a partnership, an approval or a customer account. Each row says what blocks it.
does: Reads the 100-app list (name, category, official docs hint) from the assignment.

Pass 1, research: for each app, runs targeted web searches through the Composio SDK (Tavily search tool via a Composio session), falling back to a free search backend when Composio credits ran out. It fetches the vendor's own pages and asks an LLM (Groq/Gemini, OpenAI-compatible) to fill a strict schema with one evidence URL per field.

Pass 2, verification loop: 7 automatic checks per row (evidence URL loads, is on the vendor's domain, mentions the claimed auth method and MCP, plus consistency rules such as 'sales-gated cannot be buildable=yes'). Failing rows are re-researched on the vendor's own domain by a critic model.
Writes machine-readable results (results.json / results.csv) and builds this page from them.
human: Setup: API keys and accounts (Composio, Groq, Gemini). The agent never sees the keys.
Free-tier limits: the LLM and Composio quotas ran out mid-run, so the last 18 apps were researched by the Claude agent with web search under the same schema. Those rows are labelled in the data.

An independent audit of risky claims (12 corrections, each with a source). It caught a verifier regression: pass 2 confused 'Paygent Connect' (an NMI-powered payment gateway) with an unrelated AI-cost tool, and the audit reverted it.
Ground truth for accuracy: 20 apps re-checked against vendor docs, with judgement calls (e.g. HubSpot's developer API key only covers app settings, not CRM data) and spot checks by Lavanya.
ver_note: Ground truth was re-checked against vendor docs by a separate review pass and spot-checked by a human (Lavanya). The 4 remaining misses are listed below exactly as measured; they were not retro-fitted into the score.
